paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.25:1 Rule 3.25 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.25. Remedies What is included, or not included, in the pleadings is important in terms of remedy. In Mazepa v. Embree, 2014 ABCA 438, 2014 CarswellAlta 2286, 588 A.R. 288, 14 Alta. L.R. (6th) 83, the Court said: 8 It is well-established that a trial or chambers judge should not decide a case on a matter not pleaded, and specifically should not grant remedies beyond the pleadings; the cases are noted in Sumner v PCL Constructors Inc., 2011 ABCA 326 at para. 26, 51 Alta LR (5th) 266, 515 AR 231; Dow Agrosciences Canada Inc. v Philom Bios Inc., 2007 ABCA 122, at paras. 60–2, 31 BLR (4th) 40, leave denied [2007] 3 SCR viii, and Paniccia Estate v Toal, 2012 ABCA 397 at para. 32, 71 Alta LR (5th) 411, 539 AR 349. The appellant particularly relies on statements to that effect in Wild Rose School Division No. 66 v Bert Pratch Const. Co., 1998 ABQB 831, 238 AR 339. Wild Rose was an action for the cost of constructing a school, which was brought after the school burned down. The Court made the general observation at para. 21 that the position of the parties is presumed to be set out in the pleadings, and said: “A court's jurisdiction to grant a remedy is limited by the pleadings of the party”. 9 While it is well-established that relief should be limited to what is pleaded, that rule is not absolute or truly “jurisdictional”: (a) First of all, the term “jurisdiction” has many meanings. In its very strictest sense, it refers to the court's ability to embark on the inquiry from the outset. However, it is often used to simply indicate in more general terms the boundaries of what can or should be done and not done. The limitation on the court's ability to grant the relief in Wild Rose was not jurisdictional in the strict sense. (b) Secondly, while the court is limited by the pleadings, the effect of the rule is reduced by the concurrent ability of the court to amend the pleadings at any time: R. 3.65. The Court in Wild Rose could have amended the pleadings, even during argument, if it was satisfied that there was no surprise or prejudice involved. The Court at all times had jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter, and that jurisdiction (in the strict sense) was not limited or compromised by the scope of the pleadings. (c) Thirdly, procedural requirements (and any corresponding procedural irregularities) generally do not have any effect on the court's jurisdiction. Rule 1.5(1) states: 1.5. (1) If a person contravenes or does not comply with these rules, or if there is an irregularity in a commencement document, pleading, document, affidavit or prescribed form, a party may apply to the Court (a) to cure the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity, or (b) to set aside an act, application, proceeding or other thing because of prejudice to that party arising from the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity. Procedural shortcomings are considered to be “mere irregularities”, not jurisdictional in nature: Stout Estate v Golinowski Estate, 2002 ABCA 49 at paras. 76–82, 100 Alta LR (3d) 5, 299 AR 13. (d) Fourthly, relief can sometimes be granted on conditions. It is not necessary that the specific conditions be pleaded. Here the Court was only prepared to grant exclusive possession of the matrimonial home if alternative arrangements were made for the support of the respondent. Sections 68 and 69 of the Family Law Act, RSA 2000, c. F-4.5 specifically make support obligations relevant to exclusive possession applications. The resulting order does not violate the rule that the Court is limited to the pleadings. (e) Fifthly, the parties can always consent to matters of procedure, such as amendments to the pleadings, or the resolution of the case on issues not strictly pleaded. That consent can be express or implied. Here, previous counsel for the appellant explicitly advised the original chambers judge that the appellant would waive any shortcomings in the pleadings, and the absence of any affidavit evidence on the respondent's means and needs, and invited the Court to grant spousal support. Since the Court had, at all times, jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter, there was no legal impediment to the Court giving effect to these parties' consent. It follows that it is not helpful to describe any procedural limitations identified here as “jurisdictional” in nature, and they do not render the order a “nullity”. In Wagner v. Wagner, 2014 ABCA 428, 2014 CarswellAlta 2262, 588 A.R. 218, 626 W.A.C. 218, the Court said: [27] Normally, a court should not give relief that a party has not […] expressly sought in the notice of application or pleading. Natural justice requires that the opposing party know what is being sought, and why. Usually that information is only available from the notice of application, although that is not always so. The opposing party may know what relief is sought, and why, by some other means and in enough time to marshal his or her arguments and evidence: DWH v DJR, 2013 ABCA 240 at paras 41–44, 556 AR 81. This is not to suggest that ferreting through affidavits for the issues to be decided is ideal. Relief sought should be stated with precision in a notice of application, and not left to be divined from other documents filed.

sentences.text: Time for service of statement of claim

paragraphs.text: (1) A statement of claim must be served on the defendant within one year after the date that the statement of claim is filed unless the Court, on application filed before the one-year time limit expires, grants an extension of time for service. (2) The extension of time for service under this rule must not exceed 3 months. (3) Rule 13.5 does not apply to this rule or to an extension of time ordered under this rule.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.26:1 Rule 3.26 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.26. 1. General In Urban Square Holdings Ltd. v. Del Fisher Insurance Inc., 2025 ABKB 54, Justice Price discussed the concept of “service”: [34] For there to be service, “the document must be conveyed in a context that makes it clear rights are being engaged”: 1226911 Alberta Ltd v Redecopp, 2012 ABQB 776 at para 30, citing Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corporation, 2012 ABCA 266 at para 23. [35] In Zahmol Properties Ltd v Calgary (City), 2012 ABCA 89 at para 16, the Court stated: Sometimes legal processes are commenced in order to crystallize rights, without a final decision having been made as to whether the action will be triggered by service and prosecuted. Sometimes knowledge of an action or proceeding is conveyed without intending to affect legal rights, as when a “courtesy copy” of legal process is provided. Where the knowledge of the legal process is conveyed without an intention to affect legal rights, there is generally no “service”. [citations omitted] [36] The purpose of service is for the defendant to have knowledge of the claim so that it can choose to defend itself: Goodwin v Goodwin, 2022 ABQB 520 at para 27 [Goodwin]. Service is a question of fact that does not require “a magical or formalistic ritual,” but service does require that the defendant be aware that their rights have been engaged: Goodwin at para 27, citing Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684 at para 317, aff'd 2020 ABCA 81, leave to appeal refused [2020] SCCA No 363. In Scott v. Westwinds Communities, 2021 ABCA 30, 2021 CarswellAlta 215, the Court said: [37] While not exhaustive, the general principles for a Rule 3.26 application are these: 1. A Rule 3.26 application calls upon a court to exercise its discretion. The Rule does not provide a plaintiff with a unilateral right to a three month extension. 2. The Rule is not only for the benefit of the plaintiff, as identified in Oberg, but also the defendant. It is for the benefit of the defendant in that it establishes a further type of limitation period, over and above the Limitations Act, RSA 2000, c L-12, to know if one must prepare to defend against a claim and assemble a defence. The passage of time can make this more difficult. 3. The application must be supported by an affidavit or other evidence. See Rules 6.3 and 6.11. 4. The affidavit or other evidence should set out what attempts, if any, have been made to serve the defendant and explain the reason or reasons for the lack of service within the 12 months. This does not mean there is an absolute rule that some attempt to serve must be made before bringing an application under Rule 3.26. We agree with the observations of Master Smart at para 5 of Wardill that: “Simply put the evidence provided should state ‘why you need it and what have you done?’… It makes no sense to have a deadline for service within 12 months if extensions are granted as a matter of course with not even the barest threshold of evidence required.” 5. The purpose of the renewal cannot be a stalling tactic. 6. Prejudice to the defendant, if any, is a factor to consider. In Foster v. Robb, 2011 ABQB 776, 2011 CarswellAlta 2240, Justice Tilleman said, at paragraph 6: Rules 3.26–3.28 are similar to old Rule 11 and impose a strict and mandatory limit on service of a Statement of Claim. … In the course of giving his Reasons, his Lordship referred to the submissions of counsel, and in light of his above quoted comment, would seem to agree with them. He said at paragraph 4: 4 The Defendants Leslie Robb and South Rock Ltd. apply pursuant to Rules 3.26–3.28 to dismiss the Plaintiff's case against them. Their arguments are essentially the same. They cite the following principles developed under the old Rules and assert that those principles have been incorporated into the requirements of Rules 3.26–3.28: • failure to serve on time leaves the Court with little or no option: see Martinez v. Hogeweide, 1998 ABCA 34, 209 A.R. 388; • after the Statement of Claim expires, service is impossible: see Hansraj v. Ao, 2004 ABCA 223, 354 A.R. 91, at para. 63; • no relief from forfeiture flows where the Plaintiff fails to serve the Statement of Claim in time: see Hansraj, supra, at para. 66; • exceptions to the service rule are rare: see Hiep v. Cain, 2004 ABQB 876, 365 A.R. 366, at para. 25; and • for the rare exceptions, the onus is on the Plaintiff: see Hiep, supra, at para. 34. In Padget Estate v. Padget Estate, 2014 ABQB 750, 2014 CarswellAlta 2235, Madam Justice Greckol said, at paragraph 32: 32 In my view, the weight of authority indicates that extensions brought within a year of filing the statement of claim are dealt with under Rule 3.26 and do not engage the considerations applied under Rule 3.27. … 2. Multiple defendants In Bristol-Myers Squibb Canada Co. v. Grande Prairie (City), 2023 ABCA 294, the plaintiffs sought an extension of time within which to serve a statement of claim. The extension was granted by the learned Master (as the office was then known), and an appeal of that order was dismissed King's Bench Chambers. During the course of the appeal heard in King's Bench Chambers, the learned Chambers Justice “interpreted [Scott v. Westwinds Communities, supra] as requiring evidence with respect to the specific defendant for which the extension of time to serve is sought, with no exception for cases with multiple defendants.” The Court of Appeal ultimately dismissed the appeal from the King's Bench decision, but said: [15] This Court in Westwinds at para 37 set out general principles applicable to Rule 3.26 applications: a court has discretion in deciding whether to grant an extension; the Rule is for the benefit of both plaintiff and defendant; there must be an affidavit or other evidence which should set out what attempts, if any, have been made to serve the defendant and explain why there will be lack of service within the 12 months; the purpose cannot be to stall; prejudice to the defendant, if any, is a factor to consider. [16] The Court in Westwinds expressly stated that the requirement for affidavit evidence does not mean there is an absolute rule that some attempt to serve a defendant must be made before bringing an application under Rule 3.26. In fact, the Court in Westwinds upheld the extension decision in that case despite there having been no evidence of attempts to serve. [17] The Chambers Justice interpreted Westwinds as requiring evidence with respect to the specific defendant for which the extension of time to serve is sought, with no exception for cases with multiple defendants. [18] The Court in Westwinds cited, and did not reject, the reasoning in Oberg v Foothills Provincial General Hospital, 1999 ABCA 76 at para 14 to the effect that the purpose of the affidavit is to provide enough information from which it can be inferred that the application for renewal is not simply a delay tactic. There may well be cases in which a lack of evidence with respect to a specific defendant in a multi-defendant case would be fatal to an application under Rule 3.26. However, the Court in Westwinds did not consider that scenario, nor did it purport to impose a strict requirement in that regard. …. [21] The affidavit put before the Master in this case explained that service was being attended to in relation to 45 defendants during a global pandemic. It described the progress that had been made and steps that had been taken. While it did not specifically reference steps taken in relation to the Appellants, it was open to the Master and Chambers Justice to find on the record, as they did, that the delay in serving was not a stalling tactic and that there was nothing to suggest prejudice to the Appellants. It was also open to find that the evidence provided regarding “what had been done, what still needed to be done, and why an extension was necessary” sufficed to support the application. Such a finding does not amount to creation of an “exception” applicable in all cases with multiple defendants – each Rule 3.26 application must be assessed on its own particular facts. 3. Evidence is needed In Franssen v. Thule Towing Systems LLC, 2012 ABQB 657, 2012 CarswellAlta 2003, 84 Alta. L.R. (5th) 316, Master Laycock held that evidence is required in support of an application to extend the time for service. At paragraphs 30–33, the learned Master said: [30] I disagree with the plaintiff's argument that an order to extend time for service can be made without any affidavit evidence. Firstly, some rules specifically require an affidavit in an application: see for example rules 11.25(2) (service ex juris) and 11.28(2) (substitutional service). Many rules do not specifically provided for affidavit evidence when making an application to the court. For example, an application to amend pleadings pursuant to rule 3.62(1)(b)(I) requires the court's permission. The rule does not state that an affidavit is necessary, however the case law makes it clear that evidence is required unless the amendment is trivial, obvious or clerical: Wong (Guardian and Trustee of) v. Al-Hassan 2003 ABCA 366; Hodge v. Carey Industrial Services Ltd (1997) 202 A.R. 154; Firemaster Oilfield v. Safety Boss 37 Alta. L.R. (3d) 317. A few of the other rules that do not mention affidavits include: rules 2.15 and 2.16(3) (appointing a litigation representative), 3.5 (transfer an action), 4.22 (security for costs), 4.31 (dismiss for delay where prejudice), 4.33 (dismiss for long delay), 5.11 (order to produce a record), 5.12 (failure to file affidavit of records). All of these applications would also require affidavit evidence. In Lock v. Tussman 2001 ABQB 83, Master Funduk quote the Court of Appeal in Crown Life Assurance Co. v. A.E. LePage (Ontario), C.A. 8803-0459 A.C. October 3, 1989, “no evidence-no order”. [31] Secondly, the rule requires an application to the court, so the plaintiff does not get an extension as of right. Should the Rules Committee have wanted plaintiffs to have 15 months to serve the statement of claim, the rule would be different. Should the Rules Committee have wanted the matter to be perfunctory, a clerk could have been designated to grant an extension. [32] Thirdly, any application to the court requires the exercise of judicial discretion. As the court stated in Oberg, it is a low threshold but nonetheless facts must be presented for the court to exercise its discretion. [33] It is not sufficient for counsel to merely advise the court that service has not been effected in order to obtain an extension. It is also not sufficient for the deponent of the affidavit to merely state that they are applying for an order to extend time for service. The underlying purpose of the requirement to obtain leave of the court to extend time for service remains, as described by the Court of Appeal in Oberg in paragraph 10 (supra), “a need to balance the ease of meeting a plaintiff's needs with the prevention of undue delay”. I agree with Master Smart that the test remains the same as stated in Oberg. I disagree with Master Breitkruez's conclusion in Gangl[2010 ABQB 822] that it is enough to know that service has not been effected. In 681219 Alberta Ltd. v. 1335422 Alberta Ltd., 2015 ABQB 11, 2015 CarswellAlta 31 (Master), Master Prowse said, at paragraphs 21–23: [21] The threshold for obtaining an extension of time to serve a statement of claim is low. There is no need for the plaintiff to provide evidence as to why it was unable to serve during the first one year period. There can be other grounds for seeking an extension. [22] In this case, the plaintiff did provide an explanation as to why an extension was being sought, namely the need to file an amended statement of claim, and in my view that explanation meets the low threshold required. There was a reason for the delay, and no intention to stall is apparent. [23] The defendants have not established any prejudice arising from the granting of the extension. The fact that time for service would have expired but for the extension order is not considered prejudice to the defendant arising from the granting of the order.

Al-Hassan 2003 ABCA 366; Hodge v.
Carey Industrial Services Ltd (1997) 202 A.R.
154; Firemaster Oilfield v.
Safety Boss 37 Alta.
L.R.

A few of the other rules that do not mention affidavits include: rules 2.15 and 2.16(3) (appointing a litigation representative), 3.5 (transfer an action), 4.22 (security for costs), 4.31 (dismiss for delay where prejudice), 4.33 (dismiss for long delay), 5.11 (order to produce a record), 5.12 (failure to file affidavit of records).
All of these applications would also require affidavit evidence.
In Lock v.
Tussman 2001 ABQB 83, Master Funduk quote the Court of Appeal in Crown Life Assurance Co. v.
A.E.
LePage (Ontario), C.A.
October 3, 1989, “no evidence-no order”.
[31] Secondly, the rule requires an application to the court, so the plaintiff does not get an extension as of right.
Should the Rules Committee have wanted plaintiffs to have 15 months to serve the statement of claim, the rule would be different.
Should the Rules Committee have wanted the matter to be perfunctory, a clerk could have been designated to grant an extension.
[32] Thirdly, any application to the court requires the exercise of judicial discretion.
As the court stated in Oberg, it is a low threshold but nonetheless facts must be presented for the court to exercise its discretion.
[33] It is not sufficient for counsel to merely advise the court that service has not been effected in order to obtain an extension.
It is also not sufficient for the deponent of the affidavit to merely state that they are applying for an order to extend time for service.
The underlying purpose of the requirement to obtain leave of the court to extend time for service remains, as described by the Court of Appeal in Oberg in paragraph 10
(supra), “a need to balance the ease of meeting a plaintiff's needs with the prevention of undue delay”.
I agree with Master Smart that the test remains the same as stated in Oberg.
I disagree with Master Breitkruez's conclusion in Gangl[2010 ABQB 822] that it is enough to know that service has not been effected.
In 681219 Alberta Ltd. v.
1335422 Alberta Ltd., 2015 ABQB 11, 2015 CarswellAlta 31 (Master), Master Prowse said, at paragraphs 21–23: [21] The threshold for obtaining an extension of time to serve a statement of claim is low.
There is no need for the plaintiff to provide evidence as to why it was unable to serve during the first one year period.
There can be other grounds for seeking an extension.

[22] In this case, the plaintiff did provide an explanation as to why an extension was being sought, namely the need to file an amended statement of claim, and in my view that explanation meets the low threshold required.
There was a reason for the delay, and no intention to stall is apparent.
[23] The defendants have not established any prejudice arising from the granting of the extension.
The fact that time for service would have expired but for the extension order is not considered prejudice to the defendant arising from the granting of the order.

paragraphs.text: (1) The Court may, at any time, grant an extension of time for service of a statement of claim in any of the following circumstances: (a) if a defendant, anyone purporting to be a defendant, or a lawyer or other person purporting to negotiate on behalf of a defendant, has caused the plaintiff or the plaintiff's lawyer to reasonably believe and to rely on the belief that (i) the defendant has been served, (ii) liability is not or will not be contested, or (iii) a time limit or any time period relating to the action will not be relied on or will be waived; (b) if an order for substitutional service, an order dispensing with service or an order validating service is set aside; (c) special or extraordinary circumstances exist resulting solely from the defendant's conduct or from the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action. (2) If an extension of time is granted under subrule (1), no further extension of time may be granted under this rule and rule 13.5 does not apply unless different or new circumstances described in subrule (1) are established to the Court's satisfaction.
