paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.27:1 Rule 3.27 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.27. 1. Comparison with previous rule In Sanderson Estate v. Potter, 2012 ABQB 593, 2012 CarswellAlta 1645, 550 A.R. 33, Madam Justice Read said, at paragraphs 27-28: 27 As can be seen, Rule 3.27(a) carries forward the three situations that allowed for a renewal of a Statement of Claim under Rule 11(9). There is minimal change in the wording. Rule 3.27(a) continues to recognize the common law defences of waiver or estoppel or equity based on a standstill agreement. In Foster v. Robb, 2011 ABQB 776, the Court held that Rules 3.26–3.28 are similar to old Rule 11 and that the principles developed under the Former Rules have been incorporated into the requirements of Rules 3.26–3.28. That Court held further that Rules 3.26–3.28 impose a strict and mandatory limit on the service of a statement of claim and only the rare exceptions listed in Rule 3.27 alter the limit on service. 28 Rule 3.27 also contains two new circumstances in which the renewal of a statement of claim will be allowed: when an order for substitutional service, an order dispensing with service or an order validating service is set aside (Rule 3.27(1)(b)) and when “special” or “extraordinary” circumstances exist resulting solely from the defendant's conduct or from the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action (Rule 3.27(1)(c)). Madam Justice Read noted that the general exception set out in R. 3.27(1)(c) was not in the previous rule. She said, at paragraphs 36–46: 36 There remains, however, the “general exception” set out in Rule 3.27(1)(c). This provision was not included in the Former Rules and there has been little judicial consideration of it as yet. From my research, it appears that only two reported cases have considered this section. 37 In Nixon v. Timms, op cit a process server swore in an affidavit of service that he had personally served the defendant, Timms. At later viva voce proceedings, the process server swore that the person he served had identified himself at the door as “Michael”, the first name of Mr. Timms and that he had confirmed the identity of Mr. Timms with an unnamed neighbour. The person actually served, denied under oath having said anything of the sort to the process server and had a specific recall of the process server's attendance, and told him he was not Mr. Timms. Timms testified that he was not served and was, in fact, out of the country at the time. The Court disbelieved the process server and accepted instead the other evidence, finding that the process server had sworn a false affidavit. At para 47, the Court concluded: Rule 3.27 specifically contemplates the kind of unusual and entirely unanticipated consequence of a false affidavit being sworn upon which an entire case would stand or fall. It is such an unusual and extraordinary circumstance that one could hardly imagine occurring, let alone expect it to arise shortly after the implementation of Rule 3.27 which provides the obvious remedy in order that neither party be prejudiced. 38 On the other hand, in Vanden Brink v. Russell, 2012 ABQB 523, in comments that must be seen as obiter, given his disposition of the case, a Master of the Court of Queen's Bench said this in respect to Rule 3.27: 22 With the current unsettled state of the law as to onus, a plaintiff obtaining a default judgment faces the prospect of that judgment later being set aside based on a bare denial of service by the defendant. The consequence of setting aside the judgment may be that time for service of the statement of claim will have elapsed, and the cause of action now lost due to limitations issues. While Rule 3.27(1)(b) allows for the time for service of a statement of claim to be extended where, for example, an order for substitutional service is later set aside, there is no provision to extend the time for service of a statement of claim where proof of service, upon which a default judgment has been issued, is later rejected. 39 The purpose of the Rule is to ensure that a plaintiff takes timely action in pursuing a claim and to encourage expeditious litigation. In this case, although the Statement of Claim was issued only shortly before the expiry of the relevant limitation period, the Plaintiff did take timely action in serving it. The lack of service was not caused by any inaction on the part of the Plaintiff, who relied upon the affidavit of service of his agent the process server. It was the mistake or negligence of the process server, and the reliance of the Plaintiff on this error, that resulted in Reimer not being served while the Statement of Claim was in force. However, although the parties are agreed that the affidavit of service is erroneous, unlike the situation in Nixon v. Timms, where the Court found that the affidavit of service was fraudulent, there is no evidence here of what actually happened. Nor can it be said that the circumstances of this case arose from the Defendant's conduct or the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action. 40 However, although the process server is the agent of the Plaintiff, that does not make him a party to the action. I interpret the words “person who is not a party to the action” in Rule 327(1)(c) to include a process server who has mistakenly or negligently filed an erroneous affidavit of service. 41 Process servers are commonly used in situations such as this, where an action is commenced and personal service is required. The use of a process server is, therefore, hardly a special or extraordinary circumstance. Nor, I suspect, is it a special or extraordinary circumstance for a process server to have difficulty with positive identification of someone he or she serves. The question is, do the circumstances here constitute a “special” or “extraordinary” circumstance as contemplated in Rule 327(1)(c)? 42 The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary, (5th ed) Oxford, England: Oxford University Press, 2002, defines “extraordinary” as “out of the usual or regular course or order; special”, “of a kind not usually met with, exceptional; now esp so exceptional as to provoke astonishment”. It defines “special” as “exceptional in quality or degree; unusual, out of the ordinary”. 43 In Nixon v. Timms, the process server was found to have lied on an affidavit of service. As the Court there found, such a circumstance is so rare as to be almost unimaginable. Such a circumstance is clearly “extraordinary”. Here, as in Nixon, the affidavit of service is incorrect. However, it is false and not fraudulent. The process server was mistaken in his affidavit. He did not serve Reimer as he swore he did. Although a mistaken affidavit is not the same as a fraudulent one, the mistake here could not have occurred through mere inadvertence. In the absence of any evidence that someone misled the process server, I must conclude that the process server was at least, careless and perhaps negligent. In my view, the mistaken affidavit sworn by the process server and relied upon by the Plaintiff, is a “special” circumstance such as contemplated by the Rule. 44 A decision to permit the renewal of an expired statement of claim is a discretionary one and involves some latitude. As stated by Burrows, J. in Syvenky v. Woo, 2003 ABQB 764: 14 Of course, when the situation described in Rule 11(9) exists the jurisdiction to renew the statement of claim is discretionary. The exercise of the discretion will be influenced by factors such as prejudice to the defendant and carelessness by the plaintiff. In a situation where the plaintiff's belief and reliance were brought to an end soon after the statement of claim were issued by advice that liability was in dispute, the court might well decline to renew the statement of claim. On the other end of the spectrum, if the plaintiff was induced to believe until the last few days before the expiry of the statement of claim that liability would not be contested, I expect the renewal would be easily obtained. 17 It is also significant to the exercise of the discretion that Mr. Woo suffered no prejudice as a result of Mr. Syvenky's failure to serve the statement of claim in the year. The statement of claim was in fact served, albeit substitutionally after it appeared Mr. Woo was avoiding service, within 15 months of the issuance of the statement of claim. If application had been made for a renewal of the statement of claim before the expiry of the first 12 months it would have likely been granted. The service which was effected was within the 3 months of the renewal which would have been granted. 45 The Ontario Court of Appeal has also made it clear that the key issue is prejudice to the defendant when dealing with applications to extend the time for service of an expired statement of claim. In Chiarelli et al v. Wiens (2000) 46 O.R. (3d) 780, Laskin J.A., speaking for the court, said this: 17 The court should not fix in advance rules or guidelines when an extension should be refused. Each case should be decided on its facts, focussing as the motions judge did in this case, on whether the defence is prejudiced by the delay. Undoubtedly the delay in this case—over six years from the expiry date for serving the claim—was significant, much longer than in most if not all of the decided cases where an extension has been granted. However, the motions judge recognized this delay and still found no prejudice. As I have already said, I am not persuaded that he erred in making that finding. 46 Laskin J.A. set out five factors to consider, in Chiarelli et al v. Wiens. First, the Court should not extend the time for service if to do so would prejudice the defendant. Second, the plaintiff bears the onus of demonstrating that the defendant would not be prejudiced by an extension. Third, the defendant has at least an evidentiary obligation to provide some details of prejudice which would flow from an extension of the time for service. In the face of a general allegation of prejudice, the plaintiffs cannot be expected to speculate on what witnesses or records might be relevant to the defence and then attempt to show that these witnesses and records are still available or that their unavailability will not cause prejudice. Fourth, the defendant cannot create prejudice by its failure to do something that it reasonably could have or ought to have done. Lastly, prejudice that will defeat an extension of time for service must be caused by the delay. Prejudice to the defence that exists whether or not service is delayed ordinarily is not relevant on a motion to extend the time for service: Paterson v. Lafleche, [2004] OJ No 2029 at para 14. NOTE: In her decision, Read, J. referred to the Queen's Bench decision in Nixon v. Timms, 2012 ABQB 315, 2012 CarswellAlta 2430, 540 A.R. 234. That decision was overturned in the Court of Appeal [see: Nixon v. Timms, 2013 ABCA 84, 2013 CarswellAlta 259, 544 A.R. 21; and the annotation “No Extension When Process Server Swore False Affidavit of Service” under this Rule]. Sanderson Estate v. Potter, 2012 ABQB 593, 2012 CarswellAlta 1645, 550 A.R. 33, was followed by Justice A.D. McLeod in Stremich v. Pefanis, 2016 ABQB 397, 2016 CarswellAlta 1329. In Brousseau v. Janz Estate, 2014 ABQB 136, 2014 CarswellAlta 1475, 2 Alta. L.R. (6th) 311 (Master), Master Schlosser discussed Rule 3.27 which replaced Rule 11 in the old Rules. At paragraphs 23-24: 23 There are four post-revision decisions. They appear to signify a return to an emphasis on prejudice. Unlike the earlier cases, they are (so far) uniform and not contradictory. There seems to be no sign that the discretion is used too loosely. 24 Master Wacowich lead the way in Makar v. Luedey, 2013 ABQB 189 (see also Nixon v. Timms, 2013 ABCA 84). Then came McGowan v. Lang, 2013 ABQB 699 per Schulz, M. In Marcil v. Ellefson, 2014 ABQB 18, Browne, J. summed up, saying: [50] Master Schulz in McGown v. Lang, 2013 ABQB 699, [2013] A.J. No. 1316 reviewed the law and policy and concluded at para 21 that in determining whether special circumstances exist under Rule 3.27(1)(c), the Court should: a) aim to eliminate procrastination and delay in litigation; b) consider whether there is any prejudice to any of the parties as a result of the limitation issue; c) determine if the special or extraordinary circumstances result solely from the defendant's conduct or from the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action; and d) strike an appropriate balance of the interests of the parties in order to achieve the most justice with the least injustice. [51] In Sanderson Estate v. Potter, 2012 ABQB 593 at para 46, 550 AR 33, Read J. set out factors to be considered when assessing prejudice: a) the Court should only extend the time for service where there is no prejudice to the defendant; b) the plaintiff bears the onus of proving that the defendant would not be prejudiced by the extension; c) the defendant has at least an evidentiary obligation to provide some details of prejudice which would flow from an extension of the time for service; d) the defendant cannot create prejudice by failing to do something that it reasonably could have or ought to have done; e) the prejudice must have been caused by the delay. However, it must be noted that the Master's decision in McGowan v. Lang was overturned on appeal. In McGowan v. Lang, 2014 ABQB 403, 2014 CarswellAlta 1079, 35 C.C.L.I. (5th) 285, 60 C.P.C. (7th) 160, Justice Yungwirth said, at paragraphs 28–34: 28 Rules 3.26 to 3.28 are similar to former Rule 11 and the principles developed under the former Rules have been incorporated into the requirements of Rules 3.26 to 3.28. Further, Rules 3.26–3.28 impose a strict and mandatory limit on the service of a statement of claim and only the rare exceptions listed in Rule 3.27 alter the limit on service. Sanderson Estate v Potter, 2012 ABQB 593, in referring to Foster v Robb, 2011 ABQB 776. 29 In Sanderson Estate, Read, J. noted (at para 33): There is no general equitable or discretionary power to bypass the Rules and allow for the renewal of a statement of claim when the statutory provisions are not met. The equitable power to relieve against forfeitures has no application to this situation: Hansraj v. Ao, at para 121. An expired statement of claim can only be renewed if the specific statutory requirements under the Rules are met. 30 It would appear from these decisions that the Court's discretion to grant an extension pursuant to Rule 3.27 arises only after a Plaintiff brings itself within the exceptions laid out in Rule 3.27. 31 Looking at Rule 3.27 generally, Rule 3.27(1)(a) and (b) both address circumstances where there has been reliance by the Plaintiff on circumstances which have caused the Plaintiff not to serve the Statement of Claim within the required time period. There is a connection between the lack of service and the circumstances contemplated by the Rule. Though Rule 3.27(1)(c) is intended to be more of a general exception, the reference to exceptional circumstances suggests that it will rarely be used. Further, given the nature of Rule 3.27 generally, there should be a connection between the exceptional circumstances and the lack of service. 32 In my view, the analysis under Rule 3.27(1)(c) requires a two-step process. The Plaintiff must first bring itself within the requirement that special or extraordinary circumstances exist resulting solely from the defendant's conduct or from the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action. As part of that first step, the Plaintiff must demonstrate that the special or extraordinary circumstances are connected in some way to the lack of service. 33 It is only after the first step of the analysis confirms the existence of the type of special or extraordinary circumstances contemplated by Rule 3.27(1)(c), that the court can go on to consider if is it appropriate to exercise its discretion to extend time for service 34 It is in this second step that the policy considerations of the limitations legislation and prejudice should be considered. In Marcil v. Ellefson, 2014 ABQB 18, 2014 CarswellAlta 28, 8 Alta. L.R. (6th) 88; affirmed 2014 ABCA 169, the Plaintiff sought and obtained an ex parte order extending the time for service of a Statement of Claim. The Defendant then sought an order setting aside the ex parte order. Madam Justice Browne denied the application, and, at paragraphs 35, 47–55, 58–63, 65, and 67 gave the following guidance about Rule 3.27, and in particular R. 3.27(1)(c): 35 The guidelines governing renewal or extension of the Statement of Claim outside the one year life of a claim under Rule 3.27(1) are stricter than those applicable to a Rule 3.26 extension. I will consider each potential ground under Rule 3.27(1). … 47 That leaves one possible ground for extension: special or extraordinary circumstances resulting solely from the Defendant's conduct or from the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action (Rule 3.27(1)(c)). In order to determine whether the circumstances in this case justify an extension under Rule 3.27(1)(c), it is helpful to review the relevant case law. 48 In Foster v. Robb, 2011 ABQB 776, Tilleman J. accepted that the law developed under the old rules continued to apply, and therefore the new rules imposed a “strict and mandatory limit” on service of a claim. An exception to that limit would be “rare”. 49 However, Master Wacowich noted in Makar v. Luedey, 2013 ABQB 189, [2013] A.J. No. 300 that new Rule 3.27(1) was designed to remedy inequities such as those which had arisen in cases like Hansraj v. Ao, 2004 ABCA 223, 354 AR 91. 50 In Nixon v. Timms, 2013 ABCA 84, 544 AR 21, the Court of Appeal held that the new Rule 3.27 did not apply to the claim in question which had expired prior to the new rules coming into force. The Court opined that Rule 3.27 did not create a perpetual ability to renew expired claims, but in considering whether extraordinary circumstances exist in a given case or whether to exercise discretion, a court must have regard to the policy considerations in the Limitations Act, RSA 2000, c L-12 and any prejudice arising as a result of the expiration of a particular limitation period. 51 Master Schulz in McGowan v. Lang, 2013 ABQB 699, [2013] A.J No. 1316 reviewed the law and policy and concluded at para 21 that in determining whether special circumstances exist under Rule 3.27(1)(c), the Court should: a) aim to eliminate procrastination and delay in litigation; b) consider whether there is any prejudice to any of the parties as a result of the limitation issue; c) determine if the special or extraordinary circumstances result solely from the defendant's conduct or the from the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action; and d) strike an appropriate balance of the interests of the parties in order to achieve the most justice with the least injustice. 52 In Sanderson Estate v. Potter, 2012 ABQB 593 at para 46, 550 AR 33, Read J. set out factors to be considered when assessing prejudice: a) the Court should only extend the time for service where there is no prejudice to the defendant; b) the plaintiff bears the onus of proving that the defendant would not be prejudiced by the extension; c) the defendant has at least an evidentiary obligation to provide some details of prejudice which would flow from an extension of the time for service; d) the defendant cannot create prejudice by failing to do something that it reasonably could have or ought to have done; e) the prejudice must have been caused by the delay. 53 In McGowan at paras 24 to 26, Master Schulz considered the fact that the insurance adjuster had been provided with a copy of the claim shortly after it was filed. As well, the defendant himself received notice of the claim within 19 days of the expiration of the time for service, and he was personally served within 68 days of the expiration. Master Schulz noted that this brought actual service to within the three month period allowed for an extension under Rule 3.26(2) if an application to extend the time had been brought as contemplated by that Rule. She further held that the threshold on an application under Rule 3.26 is low, and the plaintiff would almost surely have been granted an extension prior to expiry. 54 In Makar, Master Wacowich allowed an extension where the defendant learned of the claim 52 days after the renewal period had expired. The insurer had received notice (but was not served) prior to expiry, and the plaintiff had made reasonable efforts to locate the defendant. 55 As the application for extension in this case was ex parte, the Defendant had no opportunity to provide details of prejudice at that time. However, the Defendant has not, on this application to set aside, taken the opportunity she now has to put forward any details of prejudice flowing from the extension of the time for service. … 58 The Plaintiffs allege in the Amended Amended Statement of Claim that the leak in the basement was first detected in April 2011. It is not clear from the Claim at what point after the initial detection the alleged evidence of previous attempts to repair the wall was discovered. In any event, the original Statement of Claim was filed on May 8, 2012, apparently well within the two year limitation. 59 In Oberg v. Foothills Provincial General Hospital, 1999 ABCA 76, 232 AR 263, the Court of Appeal discussed the relevance of expiry of a limitation in an application for extension under old Rule 11: 22 The chambers judge erred in concluding that waiver did not apply because the defendants were prejudiced by the loss of a limitation defence. That is not the type of prejudice required. The limitation issue always exists when there is an application to extend time, but the Rules allow for an extension. Thus, the limitation can be extended in appropriate circumstances and absent prejudice. If the limitation period could be used to set aside an order extending the time limit, the Rule would be meaningless. 60 Master Wacowich took a similar approach when considering Rule 3.27 in Makar: 24 … Counsel for the Defendant suggests that [Rule 3.27] should not be used where it would involve a breach of the Limitations Act. This would be correct if the pleading itself was statute barred. In this case, the pleading is not statute barred and the only possible impediment is created by the rules for service of the Statement of Claim and extension of time for service. Rule 3.27 is specifically designed to grant relief in this type of case. 61 As in Makar, any impediment in this case is created by the rules for service, not by a breach of the Limitations Act. 62 Assuming the limitation period began (at the earliest) sometime in April 2011, the May 2013 discussions and forwarding of the claim to Mr. Oviatt occurred just outside of the two year limitation period. The reasons for limitations include the preservation of evidence, the peace and repose of society and individuals, and the economic cost of uncertainty: Institute of Law Research and Reform, Limitations, Report for Discussion No. 4, September 1986 at 2–4. There was no suggestion that evidence became unavailable after May 2013, nor that the delay in service raises significant concerns regarding the other policies. No details of prejudice have been provided by the Defendant. 63 I conclude that the policy reasons for limitations were not undermined by the extension. I further conclude that the Plaintiffs have met the onus of proving that the Defendant was not prejudiced by the extension. … 65 Had an application for substitutional service been made prior to expiry, it likely would have been granted. Similarly, as noted in McGowan, the threshold under Rule 3.26 is low and the Plaintiffs would very likely have been granted an extension if counsel had applied around that time. … 67 Defendant's counsel had knowledge of the claim at the very latest within two weeks of its expiry. The Defendant has since been personally served. On the face of it, it appears that the initial Statement of Claim was filed well within the limitation period. No prejudice has been established by the Defendant. 2. Defendant's lawyer's actions causing plaintiff's lawyer to reasonably believe service had been effected In Urban Square Holdings Ltd. v. Del Fisher Insurance Inc., 2025 ABKB 54, Justice Price said: [62] Pursuant to Rule 3.27 the Court may at any time, and in certain circumstances, grant an extension of time for service of a statement of claim. The circumstances include when a lawyer purports to negotiate on behalf of a defendant and causes the plaintiff's lawyer to reasonably believe and to rely on the belief that the defendant has been served; or when special or extraordinary circumstances exist resulting solely from the defendant's conduct or conduct from a person not a party to the action. [63] In this case, the evidence supports Urban's position that its counsel believed the Claim had been served because Fisher's counsel had requested documents that had been listed in Urban's Affidavit of Records. Making the request for the documents is an acknowledgment that the litigation is progressing. Furthermore, the communications from Fisher's counsel to Urban's counsel regarding settlement that occurred after the 1-year expiry are also evidence that supports Urban's belief that the Claim had been served or that time limits would not be strictly followed. …. [65] Once the requirements for Rule 3.27 are met, the Court must still decide whether to exercise its discretion in favour of extending the time for service. That discretion involves determining whether there is any prejudice to the defendant. I find, in this case, that there is no prejudice to Fisher in extending the time for service. It is clear, based on my findings set out earlier herein, that Fisher was fully aware of its rights and was engaging in the litigation proceedings and continued to try and negotiate settlement even after the period of time to serve the Claim had expired. 3. Defendants Who Are Deceased In Marois v. Hervieux Estate (1997), 55 Alta. L.R. (3d) 58, the Court of Appeal had before it a case in which an administrator ad litem was substituted for the deceased defendant after passage of the one year period set out in R. 11. After referring to its previous decision in Nagy v. Phillips (1996), 41 Alta. L.R. (3d) 58 (C.A.), the court said, at p. 65: This decision [Nagy] suggests that when there is a new defendant within the meaning of Rule 39(2), the one year time limit under Rule 11 begins to run anew. This interpretation seems consistent with the purpose behind s. 61(1)(c) of the Limitation of Actions Act. At p. 67, the court said: We view s. 61(1)(c) and Rule 39(2) as wholly embracing the facts of this case … The Court of Appeal concluded that the substitution of the administrator for the deceased started the R. 11 time period running again, even though the substitution occurred after the initial one year period under R. 11 had expired. The court specifically disapproved of Murray J.'s decision in Brennan v. Morris (1994), 16 Alta. L.R. (3d) 278 (Q.B.). The Limitations of Actions Act has been repealed and substituted by the Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12. This would not seem to change the result in Marois v. Hervieux Estate (1997), 55 Alta. L.R. (3d) 58, because, if the new defendant is added, the R. 3.26 limitation period starts to run again. 4. Prejudice to Defendant Widdell v. Woodman (1983), 25 Alta. L.R. (2d) 173 (C.A.), at 175, approved Cherry v. Hurtig (1981), 26 A.R. 483 (Q.B.), and states: There are two ultimate considerations—proof of prejudice to the defendants and the ends of justice in the individual case. Master Funduk noted in Eveleigh v. Royal Alexandra Hospital (1994), 163 A.R. 142 (Master), that it is difficult for a defendant to raise complaints of prejudice under R. 11 if the defendant has participated in the law suit regardless of renewal problems. At p. 145, the learned Master said: The moral of the story is that if a defendant is served with a statement of claim more than one year after it was issued and the pleading does not have a memorandum endorsed on it showing that it was renewed the defendant should not without more deliver a defence. A check of the court file is first in order. Barging ahead with a statement of defence and discoveries in such circumstances does not leave the defendant in a powerful position to raise this kind of complaint. 5. The Effect of a Failure to Renew In Martinez v. Hogeweide (1998), 209 A.R. 388 (C.A.) the Alberta Court of Appeal rejected the proposition that Shah v. Christiansen (1992), 135 A.R. 74 (C.A.) provides a court with authority to cure a failure to comply with Rule 11. At pp. 390-391, the Court said: We firmly reject any suggestion that rule 11 is optional or discretionary, or that the court can cure failure to serve under it. Shah v. Christiansen and Hi-Road Construction Ltd.… is not about the court blessing service of an expired statement of claim. P.L.J. Smith, J. relied on Martinez v. Hogeweide (1998), 209 A.R. 388 (C.A.) in Fehr v. Immaculata Hospital (1999), 253 A.R. 188 (Q.B.). In Fehr the statement of claim was issued December 9, 1987 and was served on December 10, 1997. P.L.J. Smith, J. said, at p. 192: The Court of Appeal in Martinez v. Hogeweide… clearly rejected the suggestion that rule 11 is optional or discretionary or that the court can cure the failure to serve under it. I agree with the submission of Dr. Jamieson [the defendant bringing the application] that under rule 11 the plaintiffs' action effectively is dead. The learned Chambers Judge then considered whether the defendant had waived his right to allege expiry and irregular service of the statement of claim. The Court found that the defendant had not waived his rights. Further, the Court held that “the Judicature Act… can be used, in certain circumstances, to cure a technical breach of the Rules” (p. 194). However, the Court held that the plaintiff had made a conscious decision not to pursue the action, and no special circumstances existed to justify the use of the Court's equitable jurisdiction (p. 195). Whether the court may exercise its equitable jurisdiction in matters of civil procedure is very much in doubt. See: “Use of Equitable Jurisdiction” below. In Performances Industries v. Forgues, 2006 ABCA 401, 2006 CarswellAlta 1692, 417 A.R. 189, 68 Alta. L.R. (4th) 222, the statement of claim was filed February 20, 2004, and was served February 22, 2005, which was a Sunday, and February 21, 2005 was a statutory holiday. The Court of Appeal held, at paras. 7-10: The chambers judge concluded that Rule 11(1) merely sets out an expiry date for an unserved Statement of Claim and does not impose a limitation period for serving a Statement of Claim. She also concluded that Rule 547 and s. 22(1) of the Interpretation Act were inapplicable because Performance's Statement of Claim expired without the doing of any act or thing. In our view, the chambers judge erred in law in concluding that Rule 11(1) does not impose a limitation period for serving a Statement of Claim. Although Rule 11(1) does not expressly set out such a limitation period, it indicates that a Statement of Claim will not expire if service is properly effected during the time period it provides. We are persuaded that Rule 11(1) implicitly provides for a limitation period relative to service of the Statement of Claim. As such, it is appropriate to consider the applicability of Rule 547 and s. 22 of the Interpretation Act in a case such as this. We are of the view that s. 22(1) of the Interpretation Act authorized Performance to effect service of its Statement of Claim on the date it accomplished service. That subsection applies notwithstanding that Rule 13(2) provides that service may be effected on any day, including Sunday: R. v. Wiens, [1970] A.J. No. 27 (App. Div.) at para. 1. Accordingly, we find that the chambers judge erred in law in concluding that s. 22(1) of the Interpretation Act was inapplicable in this case. In light of the conclusions we have reached regarding Rule 11(1) and s. 22(1) of the Interpretation Act, it is unnecessary for us to discuss the applicability of Rule 547. It is also unnecessary for us to consider whether the chambers judge erred in failing to grant Performance relief against forfeiture pursuant to s. 10 of the Judicature Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. J-2. 6. Use of Equitable Jurisdiction In Hansraj v. Ao, 2004 ABCA 223, 2004 CarswellAlta 849, 354 A.R. 91, 34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 199, Côté J.A. said, at pp. 213-214: The basic context is that R. 11 is mandatory, and service is impossible after the statement of claim expires at the end of 12 months (or 15 if it is renewed): Martinez v. Hogeweide et al. (1998), 209 A.R. 388, 160 W.A.C. 388, 1998 ABCA 34. The exceptions in rule 11 are narrow. Equitable principles are not usually heard of in connection with civil procedure. The court has power to grant equitable remedies: Judicature Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. J-2, various sections including s. 10. That Act says that in the case of conflict, equitable principles prevail over legal ones (s. 15), but that last section has been uniformly held not to apply to questions of civil procedure: La Grange v. McAndrew (1879), 4 Q.B.D. 210 (D.C.); Newbiggin-by-the-Sea Gas Co. v. Armstrong (1879), 13 Ch. D. 310 at pp. 311, 312 (C.A.);Friendly v. Carter (1881), 9 Ont. P.R. 41 at pp. 46-47; Barry v. Sullivan (1909), 18 Man. R. 614, 10 W.L.R. 640. Since 1914, Alberta has had no rule adopting English practice; in cases not provided for, we work by analogy to our Rules: rule 4; Barry v. Sullivan, supra. Our courts have not generally adopted Chancery procedure. Instead, they have chosen that practice which is more convenient, which is often the legal one, not the Chancery one: La Grange v. McAndrew, supra; Newbiggin v. Armstrong, supra; Friendly v. Carter, supra; Thomas v. Palin (1882), 21 Ch. D. 360 at p. 367 (C.A.); cf. dicta in Hudson Bay Co. v. Green (1881), 1 B.C.R. (Pt. 1) 247 at pp. 249, 250 (C.A.). Though equity can relieve against a forfeiture under limited circumstances, the term “forfeiture” in that context has a limited and technical meaning. Snell's Equity (30th Ed. 2000) 599, speaks of forfeiture for breach of covenant or condition where the primary object of the bargain is to secure a stated result and the provision for forfeiture is added as security for the production of that result. Usually that was done only where in substance the forfeiture was merely security for a sum of money, or leases (id. at p. 599). The doctrine of relief against forfeiture is, however, restricted to contracts concerning the transfer of proprietary or possessory rights, whether in land or other assets … not to ship charters or licenses: (id. at p. 599). The only case which the appellants cite for resort to equitable principles or relief against forfeiture is MacNeil v. Hodgin (1998), 215 A.R. 133, 1998 ABQB 145. That case is not consistent with the clear wording of rule 11 and binding cases interpreting that rule. It did precisely what that rule forbids, by invoking equitable rights to relieve against forfeitures. It cited no authority for that proposition. I have never seen any such authority (except for one case which seems to cite it obiter with approval: Fehr v. Immaculata Hospital et al. (1999), 253 A.R. 188, 1999 ABQB 865 at pp. 194-195 (paras. 29-33)). Courts have no “inherent power” to do what statutes forbid: Glover v. Minister of National Revenue (1980), 29 O.R. (2d) 392 at p. 399 (C.A.); affd [1981] 2 S.C.R. 561, 43 N.R. 271. I do not agree with, and decline to follow, the MacNeil case. 7. Sufficiency of Reasons for Renewal Application In Oberg v. Foothills Provincial General Hospital (1999), 232 A.R. 263 (C.A.), Conrad J.A. considered R. 11(6) and the standard it sets for the reasons which would justify a failure to serve the statement of claim. At p. 266, Her Ladyship said: A comparison of the former and current rule 11 demonstrates three major changes. First, under the old rule, a statement of claim could be renewed after the date for service had expired. Under the current rule, a statement of claim must be renewed before the original expiry date. Second, the old rule permitted several renewals while the current rule permits only one renewal. Third, the old rule required that sufficient reasons be given in the affidavit for the lack of service. The current rule only requires that reasons be set forth in the affidavit for the lack of service, and does not expressly include a standard or sufficiency requirement. Notwithstanding these differences, both rules serve the same purpose. The rule is designed to provide an extended period for service of a statement of claim where needed. At the same time, it seeks to eliminate the potential for protracted and unnecessary litigation delays created by extensions. Thus, there is a need to balance the ease of meeting a plaintiff's needs with the prevention of undue delay. Under the old rule an application could be made after the time expired. The timing and number of possible renewals created the potential for considerable delay. To counterbalance the ease of renewal outside of the limitation period, “sufficient” reasons were required in order to obtain a renewal and prejudice was always an important factor to consider. By imposing a high standard on the reasons for renewal, the old rule limited abuses while still serving legitimate needs. By contrast, the current rule restricts the number of renewals, and limits the time within which the renewal application must be made. The Rules allow only one three-month renewal. The application must be made within the original time for service. This is a significant change. This restriction on the number and timing of renewals prevents the delay possible under the old rule. The rule changed from “sufficient reasons” to merely “reasons”. Were the same sufficiency of reason required, the old wording could easily have been retained. It was not. The potential for excessive delay has already been limited by the timing and number of restrictions. Because renewal applications are no longer allowed outside the one-year period, the previous high standard as to the reasons for renewal is not as essential. Moreover, there is no requirement to serve a statement of claim as soon as possible, or practical, after it is issued. Service on the last day is sufficient and a party cannot be faulted for serving on that day. The need for reasons where an application is made within the time period should not be onerous. In my view, rule 11(6) merely requires that an applicant provide enough information from which it can be inferred that the application for renewal is not simply a delay tactic. An inference that the extension is more than a stalling tactic is sufficient. Keeping in mind that the rule is for the benefit of plaintiffs, that interpretation provides an appropriate balance between fairness, efficiency and expediency. 8. Where Negotiations Proceeded prior to Application to Renew The court renewed a statement of claim where negotiations had proceeded throughout and the insurers were not relying on the limitation period to dispose of the claim: Airhart v. Hunter (1985), 46 Alta. L.R. (2d) 386 (C.A.). 9. Applicability of Other Rules In the Miasek case the learned master, after a review of the authorities, concluded that the principles governing dismissal for want of prosecution are pertinent to an application for leave to take the next step and are equally pertinent to an application under R. 11. I agree generally with him in this conclusion though R. 11 contains within it an indication that the test in applications under it may be somewhat more stringent than is the test under RR. 243 or 244. That stringency is indicated by the provision that the statement of claim ceases to exist if not served within a year. Moreover, the renewal “if any sufficient reason” is shown is limited to three-month period on any one renewal. Wright v. Disposal Services Ltd. (1978), 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 173 at 178-79 (T.D.). 10. Applications to extend time to serve In Jelonek v Monterrosa-Renaud, 2022 ABKB 738, 2022 CarswellAlta 3247, Justice Feasby explained the basis upon which an extension of the time for service can be granted. He said: [1] The Rules of Court require both filing and service to commence an action.Despite this clear requirement, the practice of plaintiffs' counsel in Alberta is sometimes to file a Statement of Claim and then not serve the claim.Instead, plaintiffs' counsel may provide the Statement of Claim to a defendant, defendant's counsel, or a defendant's insurer on an informal basis.Plaintiffs' counsel's expectation in such circumstances is that settlement discussions will ensue.Sometimes settlement discussions do not occur or fall apart.When more than a year has passed since filing, the Statement of Claim has not been served, and there is no explicit standstill agreement between the parties, the defendant may seek to have the claim dismissed on the grounds that the Statement of Claim has expired.The facts of the present appeal are consistent with this archetype with the added wrinkle that after receipt of a courtesy copy of the Statement of Claim and in anticipation of service of the Statement of Claim on the Defendant, the Defendant's insurer asked to be relieved from the requirement to file a Statement of Defence and Plaintiff's counsel acceded to the request. [2] After the expiry of the one-year period from filing of the Statement of Claim, the Defendant took the position that the Statement of Claim expired because it was not served within the one-year time limit provided for by Rule 3.26.The Plaintiff applied pursuant to Rule 3.27 for an extension of the time to serve the Statement of Claim. … [3] This appeal raises the question of when it is appropriate to grant an extension of time to serve a Statement of Claim pursuant to Rule 3.27.…Where, as here, a party seeks and obtains an indulgence with respect to compliance with a time limit under the Rules of Court from an adversary, it is inequitable for that party to strictly enforce other time limits in the Rules of Court against the adversary without first giving notice of an intention to do so and an opportunity to take the required step.For the purposes of Rule 3.27, an agreement to suspend a time limit for one party gives rise to a reasonable belief that the time limit for service will not be strictly enforced against the other party in the absence of a clear indication to the contrary. …. [30] Rule 3.27(1)(a)(iii) can be viewed as a sort of codification and modification of promissory estoppel in the limited context of extensions for the filing of a Statement of Claim.Rule 3.27(1)(a)(iii) requires reasonable belief and reliance on the part of the plaintiff…. 11. Effect of Negotiations on Service—Standstill Agreements I agree with the reasons for judgment of Mr. Justice Major. When the insurers wrote to the appellant's lawyers asking that they take no further steps without ample notice to the insurers, they waived their right to rely on the failure of the appellant's lawyers to serve the renewed statement of claim during its currency. The copy of the renewed statement of claim which was delivered to the insurers by the respondent's widow showed clearly that the renewal was for three months from March 3, 1988. They knew, therefore, that it would expire on June 3, 1988. And they knew that it had not been served on the respondent. However, as late as December 19, 1988, they made an offer of settlement, which the appellant rejected. I find in this conduct confirmation of the insurers' waiver of their right to rely on the failure of the appellant's lawyers to effect proper service of the statement of claim during its currency. Cyre-Wills v. Couture (1992), 1 Alta. L.R. (3d) 209 (C.A.), at 211-12, per Hetherington J.A. In Martinez v. Hogeweide (1998), 209 A.R. 388 (C.A.), the court commented on the effect of a “standstill agreement”. At pp. 389-90 the court said: In our view not all agreements or waivers removing the need to take some step literally stop the clock so that the intervening time will be added on to the end of usual time limits… Rather, it is a matter of interpreting the correspondence or discussions in each case. . . . . . Therefore, neither the parties' words [in this case] nor equity nor necessity support a true stand-still which would automatically add the waived time to the end of the 12 months. Solicitors wishing that should say so clearly. In Dewindt v. Sandalwood Homes Ltd., 2002 ABQB 316, 2002 CarswellAlta 395, 313 A.R. 96, Clackson J. described situations in which a standstill agreement would be found. At pp. 102-103, His Lordship said: A standstill agreement is a peculiar feature of Alberta jurisprudence which is generally found only in cases where a Statement of Claim has been issued but not served within the time limited by the Rules of Court. Generally, a standstill agreement is found in the following circumstances: (a) where a Defendant has asked the Plaintiff not to take further steps on an issued claim while settlement discussions are ongoing; or (b) where a Statement of Claim has not been served, although not at the request of the Defendant and the time for service of the Statement of Claim has expired while settlement discussions were ongoing and settlement discussions continued after that expiry. . . . . . It seems to me that notwithstanding some rather loose language used from time to time in considering standstill agreements, such an agreement might be established where, by words or conduct the parties have actually or implicitly agreed to stop the clock while they talk and start the clock when they stop. A standstill agreement is not waiver because the agreement pre-dates the expiry of the time period. It pre-dates the right, interest, or privilege. A standstill agreement is not promissory estoppel because it is an agreement in the full legal sense of the word. The consideration which passes is the desire for effective, efficient, and lower cost settlements. In Kapki v. Palacz (1998), 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 145 (Q.B.); [affirmed (1999) 228 A.R. 373 (C.A.)], Mason J. said, at p. 149: Disputed standstill agreements may well be inferred by what is said and done between the parties or by how they might otherwise conduct themselves. In Wasyleshko v. Chamakese (1999), 228 A.R. 384 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal, at pp. 385-86, said: A standstill agreement obliges a plaintiff to take no further prejudicial steps in an action in consideration of ongoing settlement negotiations. Whether there is a standstill agreement and its scope are questions of fact… . . . . . … the relevant inquiry is whether the exchange of correspondence and the conduct of the parties evidences the acceptance and reliance necessary to show a standstill arrangement in respect of procedural matters pending settlement discussions. In Virji v. Kramer, 2001 ABQB 205, 2001 CarswellAlta 306, 285 A.R. 181 (Master), Master Quinn noted at p. 186: According to the Kapki decision the critical question is whether it is clear the time limits for service were not being relied on by the defendants. And at p. 387 the Court of Appeal suggested how disputes on standstill agreements might be avoided: We think it important to signal to the profession that when a standstill agreement is entered into, it would be preferable to describe it as such, and to state precisely what steps in the litgation process are waived or suspended pending the exploration of settlement. 12. Timing of Rule 3.27 Application No exact period of time can be prescribed within which a court may allow an application under rule 11(9). The court has a discretion in granting an order renewing a statement of claim and in exercising that discretion the court must look at the facts of the case. The application for an order to renew the statement of claim must be brought within a reasonable period of time having regard to all the circumstances. It would seem prudent in these cases once negotiations break down and counsel is put on notice that service is required that they will within a reasonable period of time serve the defendants or make application under rule 11(9) for renewing the statement of claim. Difficulty in locating the defendants or difficulty in serving the defendants, once located, should trigger an immediate application for an order under rule 11(9). Lundrigan v. Kundert (2001), 290 A.R. 160 (Master) at 165-166, per Master Laycock. Renewal under Rule 3.26 Operates Against All Defendants In Elizabeth Diane Yackel v. Sandra Snape/Acquest Financial Services Inc. and John Snape/A.P.I. Financial Group Inc. and Sentinel Life Management Corporation, Q.B., Doc. 0101-04928, 30th January 2006 (not reported), Lutz, J distinguished between a renewal granted under Rule 11(9) (see current R. 3.27(1)(a)) and a renewal granted under Rule 11(2) (see current R. 3.26). Under the latter, his Lordship agreed with this statement put to him in submissions: “Rule 11(2) therefore should be interpreted such that the renewal order made under that subrule operates as against all defendants.” (See p. 26 of the Reasons for Judgment). 13. Purpose of Rule 3.27 In Meyer v. Vasiu, 2002 ABQB 182, 2002 CarswellAlta 208, 313 A.R. 315, the plaintiff applied for a renewal order on the basis that an insurer had made a payment to the plaintiff pursuant to “an inter-company agreement between insurers known as the ‘fault chart’”. In dismissing the application, Belzil J. said, at pp. 317-318: I accept that the solicitor representing the Plaintiffs was unaware of the “fault chart,” but in my view, nothing turns on this. The real issue is whether or not the payments made by the insurer, for whatever reason, on the wording in Rule 11(9) caused the solicitor to reasonably believe that liability was not going to be contested. It is significant that the payments made by the insurer pre-dated the issuance of the Statement of Claim by more than one year and thus can be considered to be remote in time from the issuance of the Statement of Claim. In addition, it is uncontroverted that the solicitor for the Plaintiffs made no attempt to contact the insurer after issuance of the Statement of Claim, notwithstanding that the solicitor had previously corresponded with an employee of the insurer and that the insurer had forwarded correspondence denying liability, which correspondence was never retracted. There is no evidence that the solicitor for the Plaintiffs ever addressed his mind to the issue of serving the Statement of Claim; thus it cannot be argued that the solicitor made a conscious decision not to serve the Statement of Claim on the basis of payments previously made. On its plain wording, Rule 11(9) makes reference to a plaintiff or a plaintiff's lawyer. Surely the subjective and objective standards of what constitutes a reasonable belief are significantly higher for a lawyer compared to an unrepresented plaintiff. The Court can take judicial notice of the fact that payments are made by parties and their insurers for a variety of reasons, and there is no authority for the proposition that every payment made by a party or its insurer constitutes an admission of liability express or implied. The reality is that payments are often made on a nuisance value basis to avoid litigation. Moreover, a payment made for property damage surely does not mean that a party or its insurer thereafter agrees to pay damages for personal injury and associated claims, particularly bearing in mind that the latter amounts are often significantly larger. It is simply not reasonable for a lawyer to believe that payments for property damage, without more, are equivalent to an admission of liability or an undertaking not to contest liability. At the time the “fault chart” payments were made, there is no evidence that the insurer was or could have been aware of the quantum of the claims the Plaintiffs would be making, or that the Plaintiffs were in fact going to proceed with claims given that the insurer had denied liability up to that point in its correspondence. Up to that point, the solicitor for the Plaintiffs had not forwarded any information regarding the quantum of the claims being made by his clients. As such, the payments made by the insurer cannot be characterized as extensions of any settlement discussions which had taken place up to that point when in fact no such discussions had taken place, or from the insurer's perspective may not have even been contemplated. The mischief which Rule 11(9) is designed to address is that of lulling someone into a false sense of security and acting to their detriment by way of not serving a Statement of Claim. Rule 11(9) does not alleviate the need for a solicitor who files pleadings to be diligent in serving the same bearing in mind the requirement of Rule 11(1) to serve the Statement of Claim within 12 months. On these facts, the Plaintiffs' solicitor did not have cause to reasonably believe that liability was not going to be contested and thus should have served the statement of claim. Accordingly, the application pursuant to Rule 11(9) is dismissed with costs. In Syvenky v. Woo, 2003 ABQB 764, 2003 CarswellAlta 1280, 24 Alta. L.R. (4th) 292, a self-represented plaintiff in a motor vehicle accident claim believed, as a result of those acting for the defendant, that the defendant admitted liability. That belief ended 9 months after the issuance of the statement of claim when the defendant's insurance adjuster wrote to the plaintiff and indicated that all defences, including liability, would be pursued by the defendant. The statement of claim was served pursuant to an order for substitutional service 15 months after the claim was issued. In granting an application to renew the statement of claim, Burrows J., at pp. 295-296, said: Rule 11 creates a limitation period. Limitation provisions are to be construed strictly. “Before a person should be deprived of his or her cause of action, the language in the limiting statute should be clear and unambiguous.” (Conrad J.A., in Campbell Estate v. Fang, [1994] 9 W.W.R. 208, ¶ 10.) Rule 11(9) contains nothing to suggest that the plaintiff's belief and reliance that liability is not contested must exist at the time the statement of claim expires in order for the Court to renew the statement of claim. It says only that the belief and reliance must have been induced before the statement of claim expired. It if had been intended that the state of belief described in Rule 11(9) should exist at the time the statement of claim expired, one would expect to find words to that effect in the rule. The rule must not be construed as confining the jurisdiction to renew more narrowly than a fair reading of its words requires. Of course, when the situation described in Rule 11(9) exists the jurisdiction to renew the statement of claim is discretionary. The exercise of the discretion will be influenced by factors such as prejudice to the defendant and carelessness by the plaintiff. In a situation where the plaintiff's belief and reliance were brought to an end soon after the statement of claim was issued by advice that liability was in dispute, the court might well decline to renew the statement of claim. On the other end of the spectrum, if the plaintiff was induced to believe until the last few days before the expiry of the statement of claim that liability would not be contested, I expect the renewal would be easily obtained. 14. No Extension When Process Server Swore False Affidavit of Service In Nixon v. Timms, 2013 ABCA 84, 2013 CarswellAlta 259, 544 A.R. 21, the Plaintiff unwittingly relied on a falsely sworn affidavit of service. The Court of Appeal held that service had not been effected within the required time, and that the Statement of Claim had expired and no further action could be taken under it. At paragraphs 1–6, and 8–11, the Court said: 1 THE COURT:—The issue on this appeal is a narrow one. Can Rule 3.27 of the Alberta Rules of Court apply in this case to revive a claim that expired under R. 11 of the former Alberta Rules of Court? In our view, given the circumstances here, the answer is no. 2 A statement of claim was issued by Nixon, the respondent, against Timms, the appellant, on February 23, 2007 in which Nixon sought to recover money from Timms as a result of a failed real estate transaction. A process server hired by Nixon went to an Edmonton address to attempt service. The process server swore an affidavit that he had effected personal service on Timms at that address on December 20, 2007. 3 In reliance on the affidavit of service Timms was noted in default and judgment entered. In May 2011 Timms received notice of the judgment and moved to set it aside. 4 The trial judge found on the evidence before her that the statement of claim had not been served. Rather, the affidavit of service relied upon to note Timms in default had been sworn fraudulently and was not true. Timms was unaware of the claim until execution on the default judgment was attempted. The trial judge concluded that there had been no service of the statement of claim and set aside the default judgment. She declined to strike the claim or otherwise find it to have expired, declared that service had now been properly effected and ordered the defendant to file a defence within 20 days. Timms appeals. 5 The appellant submits that the trial judge erred in determining that an unserved statement of claim under the old rules was merely suspended, in applying the new rules of court, and in extending the time for service of the claim. We agree. 6 Under R. 11 of the former rules of court, this claim would have expired on February 23, 2008. Rule 11 did not allow for the extension of time to serve in these particular circumstances. Rule 11(1) provided that a statement of claim was in force for 12 months after it was filed. Thereafter, the rules deemed the claim to have expired. Under Rr. 11(b) and (c) the plaintiff could apply for one three month extension at any time before the 12 months had passed. No such extension was sought nor would R. 11(9) have permitted its renewal thereafter. Nevertheless, the trial judge concluded that the claim “was not a nullity” and could be renewed for an additional three months under the provisions of the new rules of court. In our view, her conclusion is incorrect. … 8 In this case, the statement of claim was never properly served. No renewal of the claim was sought while it was in force and R. 11(9), which provided for renewal in certain extraordinary circumstances, does not cover this situation. Accordingly, the statement of claim expired on its face in February 2008. The statement of claim was not suspended. The statement of claim could not be renewed under any aspect of then R. 11. When the statement of claim expired, the respondent was barred from taking any further action on the claim. Accordingly, in these circumstances the new Alberta Rules of Court cannot retroactively revive an action that expired in 2008. 9 Our view is reinforced when considered in the context of the respondent's submission that the claim had not “expired” but was suspended or capable of being renewed under R. 3.27 “at any time”. Counsel fairly conceded that although the rule involved a strict test, the trial judge's interpretation of the rule would involve endless or timeless discretion to restore a claim. In effect, the rule could be applied in these same circumstances in the year 2040 or beyond. 10 We do not accept that the drafters of R. 3.27 intended this broad a discretion or the perpetual ability to renew expired claims. We note, however, that in considering whether extraordinary circumstances exist in a given case or whether to exercise a discretion under the rule, regard must be had to the policy considerations in the Limitations Act, RSA 2000, c. L-12 and any prejudice arising as a result of the expiration of a particular limitation period. 11 The appeal must be allowed. The statement of claim expired in February 2008 and no further action can be taken under it.

Comparison with previous rule In Sanderson Estate v.
Potter, 2012 ABQB 593, 2012 CarswellAlta 1645, 550 A.R.
33, Madam Justice Read said, at paragraphs 27-28: 27 As can be seen, Rule 3.27(a) carries forward the three situations that allowed for a renewal of a Statement of Claim under Rule 11(9).
There is minimal change in the wording.
Rule 3.27(a) continues to recognize the common law defences of waiver or estoppel or equity based on a standstill agreement.
In Foster v.

Robb, 2011 ABQB 776, the Court held that Rules 3.26–3.28 are similar to old Rule 11 and that the principles developed under the Former Rules have been incorporated into the requirements of Rules 3.26–3.28.
That Court held further that Rules 3.26–3.28 impose a strict and mandatory limit on the service of a statement of claim and only the rare exceptions listed in Rule 3.27 alter the limit on service.

28 Rule 3.27 also contains two new circumstances in which the renewal of a statement of claim will be allowed: when an order for substitutional service, an order dispensing with service or an order validating service is set aside (Rule 3.27(1)(b)) and when “special” or “extraordinary” circumstances exist resulting solely from the defendant's conduct or from the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action (Rule 3.27(1)(c)).
Madam Justice Read noted that the general exception set out in R.
3.27(1)(c) was not in the previous rule.
She said, at paragraphs 36–46: 36 There remains, however, the “general exception” set out in Rule 3.27(1)(c).
This provision was not included in the Former Rules and there has been little judicial consideration of it as yet.
From my research, it appears that only two reported cases have considered this section.
37 In Nixon v.
Timms, op cit a process server swore in an affidavit of service that he had personally served the defendant, Timms.
At later viva voce proceedings, the process server swore that the person he served had identified himself at the door as “Michael”, the first name of Mr.
Timms and that he had confirmed the identity of Mr.
Timms with an unnamed neighbour.
The person actually served, denied under oath having said anything of the sort to the process server and had a specific recall of the process server's attendance, and told him he was not Mr.
Timms.
Timms testified that he was not served and was, in fact, out of the country at the time.
The Court disbelieved the process server and accepted instead the other evidence, finding that the process server had sworn a false affidavit.

At para 47, the Court concluded: Rule 3.27 specifically contemplates the kind of unusual and entirely unanticipated consequence of a false affidavit being sworn upon which an entire case would stand or fall.

It is such an unusual and extraordinary circumstance that one could hardly imagine occurring, let alone expect it to arise shortly after the implementation of Rule 3.27 which provides the obvious remedy in order that neither party be prejudiced.
38 On the other hand, in Vanden Brink v.
