The rule is designed to provide an extended period for service of a statement of claim where needed.
At the same time, it seeks to eliminate the potential for protracted and unnecessary litigation delays created by extensions.
Thus, there is a need to balance the ease of meeting a plaintiff's needs with the prevention of undue delay.
Under the old rule an application could be made after the time expired.
The timing and number of possible renewals created the potential for considerable delay.
To counterbalance the ease of renewal outside of the limitation period, “sufficient” reasons were required in order to obtain a renewal and prejudice was always an important factor to consider.
By imposing a high standard on the reasons for renewal, the old rule limited abuses while still serving legitimate needs.
By contrast, the current rule restricts the number of renewals, and limits the time within which the renewal application must be made.
The Rules allow only one three-month renewal.
The application must be made within the original time for service.
This is a significant change.
This restriction on the number and timing of renewals prevents the delay possible under the old rule.
The rule changed from “sufficient reasons” to merely “reasons”.
Were the same sufficiency of reason required, the old wording could easily have been retained.
It was not.
The potential for excessive delay has already been limited by the timing and number of restrictions.
Because renewal applications are no longer allowed outside the one-year period, the previous high standard as to the reasons for renewal is not as essential.
Moreover, there is no requirement to serve a statement of claim as soon as possible, or practical, after it is issued.
Service on the last day is sufficient and a party cannot be faulted for serving on that day.
The need for reasons where an application is made within the time period should not be onerous.
In my view, rule 11(6) merely requires that an applicant provide enough information from which it can be inferred that the application for renewal is not simply a delay tactic.
An inference that the extension is more than a stalling tactic is sufficient.
Keeping in mind that the rule is for the benefit of plaintiffs, that interpretation provides an appropriate balance between fairness, efficiency and expediency.

Where Negotiations Proceeded prior to Application to Renew The court renewed a statement of claim where negotiations had proceeded throughout and the insurers were not relying on the limitation period to dispose of the claim: Airhart v.
Hunter (1985), 46 Alta.
L.R.

Applicability of Other Rules In the Miasek case the learned master, after a review of the authorities, concluded that the principles governing dismissal for want of prosecution are pertinent to an application for leave to take the next step and are equally pertinent to an application under R.
I agree generally with him in this conclusion though R.
11 contains within it an indication that the test in applications under it may be somewhat more stringent than is the test under RR.
That stringency is indicated by the provision that the statement of claim ceases to exist if not served within a year.
Moreover, the renewal “if any sufficient reason” is shown is limited to three-month period on any one renewal.
Wright v.
Disposal Services Ltd.
L.R.

Applications to extend time to serve In Jelonek v Monterrosa-Renaud, 2022 ABKB 738, 2022 CarswellAlta 3247, Justice Feasby explained the basis upon which an extension of the time for service can be granted.

He said: [1] The Rules of Court require both filing and service to commence an action.Despite this clear requirement, the practice of plaintiffs' counsel in Alberta is sometimes to file a Statement of Claim and then not serve the claim.Instead, plaintiffs' counsel may provide the Statement of Claim to a defendant, defendant's counsel, or a defendant's insurer on an informal basis.Plaintiffs' counsel's expectation in such circumstances is that settlement discussions will ensue.Sometimes settlement discussions do not occur or fall apart.When more than a year has passed since filing, the Statement of Claim has not been served, and there is no explicit standstill agreement between the parties, the defendant may seek to have the claim dismissed on the grounds that the Statement of Claim has expired.The facts of the present appeal are consistent with this archetype with the added wrinkle that after receipt of a courtesy copy of the Statement of Claim and in anticipation of service of the Statement of Claim on the Defendant, the Defendant's insurer asked to be relieved from the requirement to file a Statement of Defence and Plaintiff's counsel acceded to the request.

[2] After the expiry of the one-year period from filing of the Statement of Claim, the Defendant took the position that the Statement of Claim expired because it was not served within the one-year time limit provided for by Rule 3.26.The Plaintiff applied pursuant to Rule 3.27 for an extension of the time to serve the Statement of Claim. … [3] This appeal raises the question of when it is appropriate to grant an extension of time to serve a Statement of Claim pursuant to Rule 3.27.…Where, as here, a party seeks and obtains an indulgence with respect to compliance with a time limit under the Rules of Court from an adversary, it is inequitable for that party to strictly enforce other time limits in the Rules of Court against the adversary without first giving notice of an intention to do so and an opportunity to take the required step.For the purposes of Rule 3.27, an agreement to suspend a time limit for one party gives rise to a reasonable belief that the time limit for service will not be strictly enforced against the other party in the absence of a clear indication to the contrary. ….

[30] Rule 3.27(1)(a)(iii) can be viewed as a sort of codification and modification of promissory estoppel in the limited context of extensions for the filing of a Statement of Claim.Rule 3.27(1)(a)(iii) requires reasonable belief and reliance on the part of the plaintiff….
Effect of Negotiations on Service—Standstill Agreements I agree with the reasons for judgment of Mr.
Justice Major.

When the insurers wrote to the appellant's lawyers asking that they take no further steps without ample notice to the insurers, they waived their right to rely on the failure of the appellant's lawyers to serve the renewed statement of claim during its currency.
The copy of the renewed statement of claim which was delivered to the insurers by the respondent's widow showed clearly that the renewal was for three months from March 3, 1988.
They knew, therefore, that it would expire on June 3, 1988.
And they knew that it had not been served on the respondent.
However, as late as December 19, 1988, they made an offer of settlement, which the appellant rejected.
I find in this conduct confirmation of the insurers' waiver of their right to rely on the failure of the appellant's lawyers to effect proper service of the statement of claim during its currency.
Cyre-Wills v.
Couture (1992), 1 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 209 (C.A.), at 211-12, per Hetherington J.A.
In Martinez v.
Hogeweide (1998), 209 A.R.
388 (C.A.), the court commented on the effect of a “standstill agreement”.
At pp.

389-90 the court said: In our view not all agreements or waivers removing the need to take some step literally stop the clock so that the intervening time will be added on to the end of usual time limits… Rather, it is a matter of interpreting the correspondence or discussions in each case. . . . . .
Therefore, neither the parties' words [in this case] nor equity nor necessity support a true stand-still which would automatically add the waived time to the end of the 12 months.
Solicitors wishing that should say so clearly.
In Dewindt v.
Sandalwood Homes Ltd., 2002 ABQB 316, 2002 CarswellAlta 395, 313 A.R.
96, Clackson J. described situations in which a standstill agreement would be found.
At pp.

102-103, His Lordship said: A standstill agreement is a peculiar feature of Alberta jurisprudence which is generally found only in cases where a Statement of Claim has been issued but not served within the time limited by the Rules of Court.
Generally, a standstill agreement is found in the following circumstances:
(a) where a Defendant has asked the Plaintiff not to take further steps on an issued claim while settlement discussions are ongoing; or

(b) where a Statement of Claim has not been served, although not at the request of the Defendant and the time for service of the Statement of Claim has expired while settlement discussions were ongoing and settlement discussions continued after that expiry. . . . . .

It seems to me that notwithstanding some rather loose language used from time to time in considering standstill agreements, such an agreement might be established where, by words or conduct the parties have actually or implicitly agreed to stop the clock while they talk and start the clock when they stop.
A standstill agreement is not waiver because the agreement pre-dates the expiry of the time period.
It pre-dates the right, interest, or privilege.
A standstill agreement is not promissory estoppel because it is an agreement in the full legal sense of the word.
The consideration which passes is the desire for effective, efficient, and lower cost settlements.
In Kapki v.
Palacz (1998), 60 Alta.
L.R.
373 (C.A.)], Mason J. said, at p.
149: Disputed standstill agreements may well be inferred by what is said and done between the parties or by how they might otherwise conduct themselves.
In Wasyleshko v.
Chamakese (1999), 228 A.R.
384 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal, at pp.
385-86, said: A standstill agreement obliges a plaintiff to take no further prejudicial steps in an action in consideration of ongoing settlement negotiations.

Whether there is a standstill agreement and its scope are questions of fact… . . . . . … the relevant inquiry is whether the exchange of correspondence and the conduct of the parties evidences the acceptance and reliance necessary to show a standstill arrangement in respect of procedural matters pending settlement discussions.
In Virji v.
Kramer, 2001 ABQB 205, 2001 CarswellAlta 306, 285 A.R.
181 (Master), Master Quinn noted at p.
186: According to the Kapki decision the critical question is whether it is clear the time limits for service were not being relied on by the defendants.
And at p.

387 the Court of Appeal suggested how disputes on standstill agreements might be avoided: We think it important to signal to the profession that when a standstill agreement is entered into, it would be preferable to describe it as such, and to state precisely what steps in the litgation process are waived or suspended pending the exploration of settlement.
Timing of Rule 3.27 Application No exact period of time can be prescribed within which a court may allow an application under rule 11(9).
The court has a discretion in granting an order renewing a statement of claim and in exercising that discretion the court must look at the facts of the case.
The application for an order to renew the statement of claim must be brought within a reasonable period of time having regard to all the circumstances.

It would seem prudent in these cases once negotiations break down and counsel is put on notice that service is required that they will within a reasonable period of time serve the defendants or make application under rule 11(9) for renewing the statement of claim.
Difficulty in locating the defendants or difficulty in serving the defendants, once located, should trigger an immediate application for an order under rule 11(9).
Lundrigan v.
Kundert (2001), 290 A.R.
160 (Master) at 165-166, per Master Laycock.
Renewal under Rule 3.26 Operates Against All Defendants In Elizabeth Diane Yackel v.
Sandra Snape/Acquest Financial Services Inc. and John Snape/A.P.I.
Financial Group Inc. and Sentinel Life Management Corporation, Q.B., Doc.
0101-04928, 30th January 2006 (not reported), Lutz, J distinguished between a renewal granted under Rule 11(9) (see current R.
3.27(1)(a)) and a renewal granted under Rule 11(2) (see current R.

Under the latter, his Lordship agreed with this statement put to him in submissions: “Rule 11(2) therefore should be interpreted such that the renewal order made under that subrule operates as against all defendants.” (See p.
26 of the Reasons for Judgment).
Purpose of Rule 3.27 In Meyer v.
Vasiu, 2002 ABQB 182, 2002 CarswellAlta 208, 313 A.R.
315, the plaintiff applied for a renewal order on the basis that an insurer had made a payment to the plaintiff pursuant to “an inter-company agreement between insurers known as the ‘fault chart’”.
In dismissing the application, Belzil J. said, at pp.
317-318: I accept that the solicitor representing the Plaintiffs was unaware of the “fault chart,” but in my view, nothing turns on this.

The real issue is whether or not the payments made by the insurer, for whatever reason, on the wording in Rule 11(9) caused the solicitor to reasonably believe that liability was not going to be contested.

It is significant that the payments made by the insurer pre-dated the issuance of the Statement of Claim by more than one year and thus can be considered to be remote in time from the issuance of the Statement of Claim.

In addition, it is uncontroverted that the solicitor for the Plaintiffs made no attempt to contact the insurer after issuance of the Statement of Claim, notwithstanding that the solicitor had previously corresponded with an employee of the insurer and that the insurer had forwarded correspondence denying liability, which correspondence was never retracted.

There is no evidence that the solicitor for the Plaintiffs ever addressed his mind to the issue of serving the Statement of Claim; thus it cannot be argued that the solicitor made a conscious decision not to serve the Statement of Claim on the basis of payments previously made.
On its plain wording, Rule 11(9) makes reference to a plaintiff or a plaintiff's lawyer.
Surely the subjective and objective standards of what constitutes a reasonable belief are significantly higher for a lawyer compared to an unrepresented plaintiff.

The Court can take judicial notice of the fact that payments are made by parties and their insurers for a variety of reasons, and there is no authority for the proposition that every payment made by a party or its insurer constitutes an admission of liability express or implied.
The reality is that payments are often made on a nuisance value basis to avoid litigation.

Moreover, a payment made for property damage surely does not mean that a party or its insurer thereafter agrees to pay damages for personal injury and associated claims, particularly bearing in mind that the latter amounts are often significantly larger.
It is simply not reasonable for a lawyer to believe that payments for property damage, without more, are equivalent to an admission of liability or an undertaking not to contest liability.

At the time the “fault chart” payments were made, there is no evidence that the insurer was or could have been aware of the quantum of the claims the Plaintiffs would be making, or that the Plaintiffs were in fact going to proceed with claims given that the insurer had denied liability up to that point in its correspondence.
Up to that point, the solicitor for the Plaintiffs had not forwarded any information regarding the quantum of the claims being made by his clients.

As such, the payments made by the insurer cannot be characterized as extensions of any settlement discussions which had taken place up to that point when in fact no such discussions had taken place, or from the insurer's perspective may not have even been contemplated.
The mischief which Rule 11(9) is designed to address is that of lulling someone into a false sense of security and acting to their detriment by way of not serving a Statement of Claim.

Rule 11(9) does not alleviate the need for a solicitor who files pleadings to be diligent in serving the same bearing in mind the requirement of Rule 11(1) to serve the Statement of Claim within 12 months.
On these facts, the Plaintiffs' solicitor did not have cause to reasonably believe that liability was not going to be contested and thus should have served the statement of claim.
Accordingly, the application pursuant to Rule 11(9) is dismissed with costs.
In Syvenky v.
Woo, 2003 ABQB 764, 2003 CarswellAlta 1280, 24 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 292, a self-represented plaintiff in a motor vehicle accident claim believed, as a result of those acting for the defendant, that the defendant admitted liability.

That belief ended 9 months after the issuance of the statement of claim when the defendant's insurance adjuster wrote to the plaintiff and indicated that all defences, including liability, would be pursued by the defendant.
The statement of claim was served pursuant to an order for substitutional service 15 months after the claim was issued.
In granting an application to renew the statement of claim, Burrows J., at pp.
295-296, said: Rule 11 creates a limitation period.

Limitation provisions are to be construed strictly. “Before a person should be deprived of his or her cause of action, the language in the limiting statute should be clear and unambiguous.” (Conrad J.A., in Campbell Estate v.

208, ¶ 10.) Rule 11(9) contains nothing to suggest that the plaintiff's belief and reliance that liability is not contested must exist at the time the statement of claim expires in order for the Court to renew the statement of claim.
It says only that the belief and reliance must have been induced before the statement of claim expired.
It if had been intended that the state of belief described in Rule 11(9) should exist at the time the statement of claim expired, one would expect to find words to that effect in the rule.
The rule must not be construed as confining the jurisdiction to renew more narrowly than a fair reading of its words requires.
Of course, when the situation described in Rule 11(9) exists the jurisdiction to renew the statement of claim is discretionary.
The exercise of the discretion will be influenced by factors such as prejudice to the defendant and carelessness by the plaintiff.

In a situation where the plaintiff's belief and reliance were brought to an end soon after the statement of claim was issued by advice that liability was in dispute, the court might well decline to renew the statement of claim.

On the other end of the spectrum, if the plaintiff was induced to believe until the last few days before the expiry of the statement of claim that liability would not be contested, I expect the renewal would be easily obtained.
No Extension When Process Server Swore False Affidavit of Service In Nixon v.
Timms, 2013 ABCA 84, 2013 CarswellAlta 259, 544 A.R.
21, the Plaintiff unwittingly relied on a falsely sworn affidavit of service.
The Court of Appeal held that service had not been effected within the required time, and that the Statement of Claim had expired and no further action could be taken under it.
At paragraphs 1–6, and 8–11, the Court said: 1 THE COURT:—The issue on this appeal is a narrow one.
Can Rule 3.27 of the Alberta Rules of Court apply in this case to revive a claim that expired under R.
11 of the former Alberta Rules of Court?
In our view, given the circumstances here, the answer is no.

2 A statement of claim was issued by Nixon, the respondent, against Timms, the appellant, on February 23, 2007 in which Nixon sought to recover money from Timms as a result of a failed real estate transaction.
A process server hired by Nixon went to an Edmonton address to attempt service.
The process server swore an affidavit that he had effected personal service on Timms at that address on December 20, 2007.
3 In reliance on the affidavit of service Timms was noted in default and judgment entered.
In May 2011 Timms received notice of the judgment and moved to set it aside.
4 The trial judge found on the evidence before her that the statement of claim had not been served.
Rather, the affidavit of service relied upon to note Timms in default had been sworn fraudulently and was not true.
Timms was unaware of the claim until execution on the default judgment was attempted.
The trial judge concluded that there had been no service of the statement of claim and set aside the default judgment.
She declined to strike the claim or otherwise find it to have expired, declared that service had now been properly effected and ordered the defendant to file a defence within 20 days.
Timms appeals.

5 The appellant submits that the trial judge erred in determining that an unserved statement of claim under the old rules was merely suspended, in applying the new rules of court, and in extending the time for service of the claim.
We agree.
6 Under R.
11 of the former rules of court, this claim would have expired on February 23, 2008.
Rule 11 did not allow for the extension of time to serve in these particular circumstances.
Rule 11(1) provided that a statement of claim was in force for 12 months after it was filed.
Thereafter, the rules deemed the claim to have expired.
Under Rr.
11(b) and (c) the plaintiff could apply for one three month extension at any time before the 12 months had passed.
No such extension was sought nor would R.
11(9) have permitted its renewal thereafter.
Nevertheless, the trial judge concluded that the claim “was not a nullity” and could be renewed for an additional three months under the provisions of the new rules of court.
In our view, her conclusion is incorrect. … 8 In this case, the statement of claim was never properly served.
No renewal of the claim was sought while it was in force and R.
11(9), which provided for renewal in certain extraordinary circumstances, does not cover this situation.
Accordingly, the statement of claim expired on its face in February 2008.
The statement of claim was not suspended.
The statement of claim could not be renewed under any aspect of then R.
When the statement of claim expired, the respondent was barred from taking any further action on the claim.
Accordingly, in these circumstances the new Alberta Rules of Court cannot retroactively revive an action that expired in 2008.
9 Our view is reinforced when considered in the context of the respondent's submission that the claim had not “expired” but was suspended or capable of being renewed under R.
3.27 “at any time”.
Counsel fairly conceded that although the rule involved a strict test, the trial judge's interpretation of the rule would involve endless or timeless discretion to restore a claim.
In effect, the rule could be applied in these same circumstances in the year 2040 or beyond.
10 We do not accept that the drafters of R.
3.27 intended this broad a discretion or the perpetual ability to renew expired claims.

We note, however, that in considering whether extraordinary circumstances exist in a given case or whether to exercise a discretion under the rule, regard must be had to the policy considerations in the Limitations Act, RSA 2000, c.
L-12 and any prejudice arising as a result of the expiration of a particular limitation period.
11 The appeal must be allowed.
The statement of claim expired in February 2008 and no further action can be taken under it.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.31:1 Rule 3.31 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.31. 1. Effect of Late Delivery Do not ignore a late statement of defence. … a defence delivered after the proper time cannot be disregarded even though it is not delivered until after the plaintiff has served notice of motion for judgment… In such a case the court will have regard to the contents of the defence delivered out of time and deal with the case in such a manner that justice can be done…Aldridge v. Dogwood Sales Agencies Ltd. (1958), 25 W.W.R. 591 at 591-92 (B.C. S.C.). 2. One Cannot Deliver a Statement of Defence after Judgment A defendant cannot deliver a defence after the action has gone to judgment. A judgment closes out belated defences, on the simple ground that a judgment creates issue estoppel for any issues that were or could have been raised in the action…Alberta Treasury Branches v. Naber (1994), 161 A.R. 393 (Master), at 397, per Master Funduk. 3. Filing Defence before Service of Claim In Martin v. Dukart (1997), 58 Alta. L.R. (3d) 171 (Master), the plaintiff filed, but did not serve, a statement of claim in relation to a motor vehicle accident. The defendant learned of the action, filed and served a statement of defence, and, among other things, served the plaintiff with an appointment for examinations for discovery. The defendant applied for an order compelling the plaintiff to attend for discovery. At pp. 173-74, Master Alberstat said: There may be good reason why a plaintiff holds off service of the statement of claim. In this case the plaintiff wanted the injury claimed to resolve itself before proceeding. The statement of claim may be issued to preserve a cause of action in the face of a limitation period, but it may be that more time is required to investigate the circumstances. The question therefore is whether or not a defendant learning of a claim can defend without being formally served. A defendant can file a defence at any time he or she has notice of a claim. The plaintiff's action at that time, if the plaintiff does not want to proceed, would be to apply to the court for a stay, which if the circumstances dictate would be granted. There are situations that can justify a stay of a plaintiff's own action such as requiring an injury to resolve itself before proceeding. In such a case the filing of the statement of claim to preserve the action might be justified. The court in such a situation has the discretion to stay [an] action if it feels it is justified. Another situation which is more common is the commencement of proceedings in debt. In such a case the defendant may be prejudiced by having a potential claim reported to credit reporting agencies. A defendant in such a case in the absence of service of the statement of claim can file a defence and press on to trial if the debt is denied. If a defendant files a defence without having been served a statement of claim and the plaintiff decides to discontinue the action the question then arises as to the allocation of costs. If that problem does arise the court has complete discretion and may allow a discontinuance without costs but may, if the case warrants it, award costs to a defendant.

Effect of Late Delivery Do not ignore a late statement of defence. … a defence delivered after the proper time cannot be disregarded even though it is not delivered until after the plaintiff has served notice of motion for judgment… In such a case the court will have regard to the contents of the defence delivered out of time and deal with the case in such a manner that justice can be done…Aldridge v.
Dogwood Sales Agencies Ltd.
One Cannot Deliver a Statement of Defence after Judgment A defendant cannot deliver a defence after the action has gone to judgment.
A judgment closes out belated defences, on the simple ground that a judgment creates issue estoppel for any issues that were or could have been raised in the action…Alberta Treasury Branches v.
393 (Master), at 397, per Master Funduk.
Filing Defence before Service of Claim In Martin v.
Dukart (1997), 58 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 171 (Master), the plaintiff filed, but did not serve, a statement of claim in relation to a motor vehicle accident.
The defendant learned of the action, filed and served a statement of defence, and, among other things, served the plaintiff with an appointment for examinations for discovery.
The defendant applied for an order compelling the plaintiff to attend for discovery.
At pp.
173-74, Master Alberstat said: There may be good reason why a plaintiff holds off service of the statement of claim.
In this case the plaintiff wanted the injury claimed to resolve itself before proceeding.
The statement of claim may be issued to preserve a cause of action in the face of a limitation period, but it may be that more time is required to investigate the circumstances.
The question therefore is whether or not a defendant learning of a claim can defend without being formally served.
A defendant can file a defence at any time he or she has notice of a claim.
The plaintiff's action at that time, if the plaintiff does not want to proceed, would be to apply to the court for a stay, which if the circumstances dictate would be granted.
There are situations that can justify a stay of a plaintiff's own action such as requiring an injury to resolve itself before proceeding.
In such a case the filing of the statement of claim to preserve the action might be justified.
The court in such a situation has the discretion to stay [an] action if it feels it is justified.
Another situation which is more common is the commencement of proceedings in debt.
In such a case the defendant may be prejudiced by having a potential claim reported to credit reporting agencies.
A defendant in such a case in the absence of service of the statement of claim can file a defence and press on to trial if the debt is denied.
If a defendant files a defence without having been served a statement of claim and the plaintiff decides to discontinue the action the question then arises as to the allocation of costs.
If that problem does arise the court has complete discretion and may allow a discontinuance without costs but may, if the case warrants it, award costs to a defendant.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.33:1 Rule 3.33 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.33. In Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada, 2004 ABCA 279, 2004 CarswellAlta 1188, 354 A.R. 365, 33 Alta. L.R. (4th) 231, the Court discussed what may be included in a reply. At pp. 368-369, the Court said: … Alberta's Rules of Court define a reply at rule 5(1)(o) as “a statement by which the plaintiff answers the defendant's statement of defence” but the Rules do not specify requirements for a reply. However, the reply, like all pleadings, must meet the requirement of rule 110(2) which provides: 110. (2) No pleading shall, except by way of amendment, raise any new ground of claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the party pleading it. Stevenson and Côté in Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2004 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2004) at p. 96, comment that rule 110(2) says that “a reply is not the place to put a cause of action”. Similarly, Goldrein and Jacob in their text, Pleadings: Principles and Practice (London: Sweet and Maxwell, 1990) at p. 161-2, note that a plaintiff must not in a reply make any allegations of fact or raise any new ground of claim inconsistent with the statement of claim. They agree with Stevenson and Côté that a new cause of action is to be pleaded by amending the statement of claim. New causes of action were not permitted in a reply in Udovitch Estate v. Helm Estate (2000), 276 A.R. 147, 2000 ABQB 796, and Kaup v. Weir et al. (1998), 224 A.R. 347 (Q.B.). This requirement does not change because of an amended statement of defence. If the reply raises a new cause of action, then it is an error independent of anything contained in the respondents' pleadings. The Chambers judge was not required to consider the effect of the amended statement of defence when determining whether the reply raised new causes of action. In Laughren v. Rosetown Union Hospital Board (1966), 56 W.W.R. (N.S.) 165 (Sask. Q.B.), relying on Bullen & Leake's Precedents of Pleadings (11th Ed.), at p. 693, four purposes for a reply were listed at p. 170: a) to admit some of the facts alleged in the defence, or to meet them by asserting new and additional facts; b) to plead an objection in point of law; c) to plead in answer to the defence that it mistakes the causes of action; and d) if the defendants has pleaded a counterclaim which the plaintiff desires to contest, to deal with allegations of fact in the counterclaim.

paragraphs.text: 3.34. Demand for notice by defendant
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Demand for notice by defendant

paragraphs.text: (1) If the defendant files a demand for notice, the demand must be in Form 13. (2) The defendant must file the demand for notice and serve it on the plaintiff within the applicable time after service of the statement of claim on the defendant. (3) The applicable time is (a) 20 days if service is effected in Alberta, (b) one month if service is effected outside Alberta but in Canada, and (c) 2 months if service is effected outside Canada. (4) If the defendant files a demand for notice and serves it on the plaintiff, the defendant must be served with notice of any application or proceeding in which the defendant is named as respondent, but filing and service of the notice does not give the defendant a right to contest liability. (5) If a defendant files a demand for notice and serves it on the plaintiff, the defendant may subsequently file a statement of defence only with the Court's permission. (6) Judgment or an order may be given against a defendant who has filed and served a demand for notice only if (a) the plaintiff applies to the Court for judgment or an order, and (b) notice of the application is served on the defendant.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.34:1 Rule 3.34 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.34. 1. Amendment Rules Govern Withdrawal of Demand of Notice In my opinion to withdraw a Demand of Notice and replace it by a Statement of Defence is no different than the ordinary amendment of a pleading and the same rules apply. It is trite law that an amendment will be permitted where it can be made without prejudice to the opposite party or where the prejudice can be compensated with costs. When an admission has been made, as was done here by filing a Demand of Notice or where merely technical defences have been omitted and are now sought to be advanced or where there has been long delay, the court will be less likely to grant the amendment. All of the factors either for or against the exercise of the discretion to permit amendment must be weighed and that decision made which will best do justice between the parties. Canada Permanent Trust Co. v. King Art Developments Ltd. (1984), 52 A.R. 139 at 146-47 C.A. 2. Purpose of Demand of Notice Its purpose … is to give to a defendant who admits his liability under the cause of action sued on a chance to see that he is not held for more than he should be for that purpose and to present, if necessary, to the Court anything that may be helpful to it in that respect. Stone v. Vulcan Municipal Hospital District, [1930] 1 W.W.R. 839 (Alta. T.D.), per Walsh J., quoted with approval in Lupkoski v. Lupkoski, [1974] 3 W.W.R. 377 (Alta. C.A.), which was quoted with approval in Canada Permanent Trust Co. v. King Art Developments Ltd. (1984), 52 A.R. 139 at 146 (C.A.). 3. Effect of Demand of Notice The demand of notice results in the admission of liability by the defendant but it preserves the defendant's ability to dispute the amount sought. … where damages only were in question, by filing a demand of notice, a defendant would be entitled to have notice of a taking of account on a mortgage. Lupkoski v. Lupkoski, [1974] 3 W.W.R. 377 (Alta. C.A.), at 378, per McDermind J., paraphrasing Canadian Mortgage Investment Co. v. Baird (1916), 10 W.W.R. 1195 (Alta. T.D.). 4. Right of Defendant The defendant is entitled to be heard on the motion required by R. 146. As Walsh J. stated in Stone v. Vulcan Municipal Hospital District, [1930] 1 W.W.R. 839 (Alta. T.D.), as quoted in Lupkoski v. Lupkoski, [1974] 3 W.W.R. 377 (Alta. C.A.), at 379: The defendant having given its demand of notice became entitled to ‘notice of all motions against him subsequently made in the action’… The only purpose of this can be to give him an opportunity to appear upon it and his appearance would be a futile thing if he could not be heard upon the motion. This goes so far as to permit cross-examination and the calling of evidence on the issue of quantum: Lupkoski v. Lupkoski, [1974] 3 W.W.R. 377 (Alta. C.A.), at p. 381. 5. When Leave Required Master Funduk says in Alberta Treasury Branches v. Naber (1994), 161 A.R. 393 (Master), at p. 397: To deliver a statement of defence in place of a demand of notice is in essence an amendment of a pleading … Filing a statement of defence after filing a demand of notice may only occur with leave. The defendants … who initially filed demands of notice now wish to withdraw the demands of notice and to file statements of defence. It is my view that they are not entitled to do so as of right, but that leave may be granted to permit the filing of statements of defence. Bell v. Grande Mountain Apartments (1983), 29 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 (Q.B.), at 273, per McFadyen J. One must therefore apply for leave to replace the demand of notice with a statement of defence. The application is analogous to an application under R. 158 “to set aside a noting in default and to permit the filing of a defence. The procedure applicable thereto can be applied to this application.” See Bell v. Grande Mountain Apartments (1983), 29 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 (Q.B.), at p. 277. The defendants must also show that they have a good defence on the merits. It would be entirely unproductive to permit the filing of a statement of defence in circumstances where a summary judgment application would be granted should a statement of defence be filed. Bell v. Grande Mountain Apartments, supra, at 277.

paragraphs.text: 3.35. Judgment or order by agreement
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Judgment or order by agreement

paragraphs.text: (1) If a lawyer files a statement of defence or demand for notice on behalf of a defendant, no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties unless the defendant's lawyer of record is a party to the agreement or consents to the agreement. (2) If a defendant (a) does not file a statement of defence or a demand for notice, (b) files a statement of defence or demand for notice in person or by a lawyer who has ceased to be the defendant's lawyer of record, or (c) is not represented by a lawyer of record, no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties unless the defendant's agreement, with an affidavit of execution, is filed with the application for the judgment or order. (3) If a lawyer files a statement of claim on behalf of a plaintiff, no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties unless the plaintiff's lawyer of record is a party to the agreement or consents to the agreement. (4) If a plaintiff (a) files a statement of claim in person or by a lawyer who has ceased to be the plaintiff's lawyer of record, or (b) is not represented by a lawyer of record, no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties unless the plaintiff's agreement, with an affidavit of execution, is filed with the application for the judgment or order.
